findings.title: Denial cache key does not include identity type
findings.body: Check builds the negative-cache key from namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, and parent. UserUID is only the identifier part of the subject and does not include the identity type returned by validateSubject. Different identity types can share the same identifier, for example anonymous:0 and render:0 in the tests, or user/service-account numeric identifiers. Because the denial cache is consulted before identity-specific permission logic, a denial cached for one identity can be returned for another. For example, an anonymous denial for dashboards:read on a dashboard can cause the render service to be denied even though it is hard-coded to allow dashboard reads. Include IdentityType, or the full subject, in the denial cache key and canonicalize the identifier.

findings.title: Denial cache key can collide because fields are joined with underscores
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent with underscore separators and without escaping. These fields can be empty and identifiers such as dashboard/folder UIDs may contain underscores, making the boundary between fields ambiguous. Different (user, action, name, parent) tuples can therefore produce the same cache key, causing a denial entry for one tuple to incorrectly deny another tuple. Use an unambiguous key encoding, such as escaped fields, base64/hash encoding, or a separator that cannot appear in the values.

findings.title: Cached denial can hide newly granted permissions for its TTL
findings.body: A denied Check is stored in permDenialCache for 30 seconds. Subsequent checks hit this entry and return deny before the new logic that re-queries the database when a cached permission set lacks the requested resource. If a permission is granted or a resource is created immediately after a check was denied for the same namespace/user/action/name/parent, the user can remain denied until the TTL expires. This can still break immediate access to newly created dashboards or folders in races or with client-generated UIDs. Consider invalidating negative entries on permission changes or avoiding negative caching for create/read-after-create paths.

findings.title: Denial-cache override test uses a deny permission instead of an allow
findings.body: The test sets permCache to map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': false} while the comment says it should allow access to prove the denial cache entry is used. With a false permission the request would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored, so the test does not verify that a denial-cache entry overrides a positive cached permission. The cached permission should be set to true to make the assertion meaningful.
